title: Abdominal pain in pregnancy
summary: Any abdominal, side, or pelvic pain in pregnancy — includes ruling out ectopic, ovarian cyst accident, appendicitis, abruption, UTI, and labour before reassuring round ligament pain, pelvic girdle pain, or constipation.
redFlags: Signs of shock or collapse (faint/dizzy, racing heart, clammy, confused) — emergency, regardless of cause.
Severe, constant pain — not coming and going — especially with a very hard/tense tummy.
One-sided pain or shoulder-tip pain under 14 weeks — think ectopic.
Sudden severe one-sided pain with nausea/vomiting, especially with a known ovarian cyst, fibroid, or fertility treatment — think ovarian cyst accident (torsion/rupture).

blocks.heading: Shock or collapse
bullets: Call 999 / put out an emergency call per local protocol — do not drive her in.
Consider ectopic rupture, concealed placental abruption, ovarian cyst accident (torsion/rupture), or another acute abdominal emergency — do not wait to determine the exact cause before escalating.
Do not perform a digital vaginal examination — placenta praevia has not been excluded.
IV access, bloods including group & save/crossmatch, senior obstetric and (if not clearly obstetric) general surgical input.
See the Maternal collapse emergency drill for full A–E actions.

blocks.heading: Severe, constant pain — suspected acute abdomen or concealed abruption
bullets: Arrange immediate emergency transfer — do not wait for a routine slot.

At 24+ weeks: treat as suspected placental abruption even without visible bleeding (abruption can be concealed) — see Vaginal bleeding and Major obstetric haemorrhage; continuous fetal monitoring once available.

Under 24 weeks: consider ectopic rupture, ovarian cyst accident (torsion or rupture), or another surgical abdominal emergency — arrange emergency gynaecology/surgical assessment alongside obstetric review.
Do not perform a digital vaginal examination until placenta praevia excluded.

blocks.heading: With vaginal bleeding
bullets: Also work through the Vaginal bleeding in pregnancy topic — treat as antepartum haemorrhage (24+ weeks) or early-pregnancy bleeding (under 24 weeks) according to gestation; the same red-flag causes apply (abruption, ectopic, praevia).
Do not perform a digital vaginal examination until placenta praevia excluded.
Arrange same-day assessment with observations, fetal assessment as appropriate for gestation, and ultrasound.

blocks.heading: Suspected ectopic pregnancy (under 14 weeks)
bullets: One-sided pain, or pain at the tip of the shoulder.
Arrange emergency transfer for assessment — do not wait for a routine early pregnancy unit slot.
Early pregnancy unit or gynaecology emergency assessment with urgent ultrasound and beta-hCG.
Call 999 immediately if any signs of shock/collapse develop at any point.

blocks.heading: Possible ovarian cyst accident (torsion or rupture) — any gestation
bullets: Sudden severe onset, often one-sided, possibly with nausea/vomiting — particularly with a known ovarian cyst, fibroid, or fertility treatment; cannot be excluded by phone.
Arrange same-day joint obstetric and gynaecology assessment — ovarian torsion is time-critical for ovary-conserving surgery, so a low threshold for review is appropriate.
Pelvic/transvaginal ultrasound with Doppler flow assessment where available.
Ovarian cysts are more common in the first trimester (e.g. corpus luteal cysts) and with assisted conception, but torsion can occur at any gestation.
If signs of shock develop at any point (suggesting rupture with bleeding), escalate immediately as a maternal emergency.

blocks.heading: Possible appendicitis — any gestation
bullets: Pain in the lower right side of the tummy (early) or right side/atypical site (later), with loss of appetite, nausea/vomiting, or temperature; cannot be safely excluded remotely.
Arrange same-day joint obstetric and general surgical assessment.

Presentation is often atypical in pregnancy — as the uterus enlarges the appendix is displaced upward and laterally, so pain may not be in the classic right iliac fossa position, especially later in pregnancy — VERIFY this against a surgical reference before teaching it as fact.
Bloods (FBC, CRP) and urinalysis to help exclude a urinary cause; consider ultrasound; do not delay surgical review awaiting results.
Missed or delayed diagnosis carries higher rates of perforation and fetal loss — a low threshold for review is appropriate.

blocks.heading: Possible UTI / pyelonephritis
bullets: Fever, loin/flank pain, pain or burning passing urine, or needing to pass urine more often than usual.
Arrange same-day assessment — urine dipstick and midstream urine sample sent for culture.

If fever, loin pain, rigors, or feeling systemically unwell: treat as suspected pyelonephritis — admit, IV antibiotics per local protocol, consider a full sepsis screen (see Sepsis emergency drill if red-flag features).
If lower urinary symptoms only, without fever or systemic upset: treat per local UTI-in-pregnancy protocol — VERIFY current first-line antibiotic choice locally.

blocks.heading: Possible labour
bullets: Regular tightenings, coming and going in a pattern, getting closer together.

Under 37 weeks (suspected preterm labour): same-day assessment — speculum/vaginal exam for cervical change per local protocol; discuss antenatal corticosteroids and magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection if very preterm — VERIFY exact gestation cut-offs and dosing locally; consider tocolysis and in-utero transfer if the unit lacks appropriate neonatal cot capacity.

37 weeks or more (possible labour at term): give standard advice on when to come in (e.g. regular strong contractions roughly every 3–5 minutes lasting 45–60 seconds, or waters breaking, or any bleeding) — VERIFY exact local admission criteria, as these vary by unit and parity.

blocks.heading: With headache, visual disturbance, or epigastric pain
bullets: This overlaps with the pre-eclampsia screen — work through the Headache, visual disturbance or epigastric pain topic for full BP-banded guidance.
In the meantime, arrange same-day blood pressure and urine protein check, plus pre-eclampsia bloods (FBC, U&E, LFTs) and fetal assessment (CTG).

blocks.heading: Likely pregnancy-related pelvic girdle pain (SPD)
bullets: Pain over the pubic bone, groin, hips, or lower back — worse walking, climbing stairs, standing on one leg, or turning over in bed, sometimes with clicking or grinding.
Reassure this is common in pregnancy and usually mechanical, not a sign of a problem with the baby.
Refer to obstetric/pelvic health physiotherapy for assessment, exercises, and pelvic support belt advice — VERIFY local referral route and waiting time.
Practical advice: keep knees together getting in/out of a car or turning in bed, avoid provoking activities (wide-leg movements, standing on one leg to dress), take stairs one at a time.

blocks.heading: Likely constipation
bullets: Bloating, straining, infrequent or hard stools, with nothing else concerning.
Reassure that constipation is common in pregnancy (hormonal effects on the bowel and, later, pressure from the growing uterus) and is not usually a sign of a problem.
Advise increasing fluid and fibre intake and gentle activity; signpost to local/BNF guidance if a laxative is being considered rather than giving medication advice directly.

blocks.heading: Likely round ligament or musculoskeletal pain
bullets: Mild, sharp or aching pain, worse on standing, moving, or coughing, low in the tummy or groin, with nothing else concerning.
Reassure this is commonly round ligament or musculoskeletal stretching pain and is not usually a sign of a problem.
Advise simple measures — rest, gentle movement, warmth; signpost to local/BNF guidance for analgesia rather than giving medication advice directly.

blocks.heading: Cause unclear — still worth a face-to-face check
bullets: Red-flag causes screened and not currently present, but the cause is not clearly benign — arrange face-to-face assessment.

Abdominal (and, if indicated, pelvic) examination, urinalysis, fetal assessment (CTG if appropriate for gestation), BP check, and consider ultrasound if pain persists, is severe, or the diagnosis remains unclear.
Reconsider ectopic, ovarian cyst accident, appendicitis, abruption, labour, UTI, and pre-eclampsia if the picture changes.

blocks.heading: Safety-netting to give (all non-emergency outcomes)
bullets: Contact the unit again immediately — any time — if pain becomes severe, constant, or one-sided, bleeding starts, fever develops, movements reduce, or she feels faint or generally unwell.
Come back at any time, however many times, if still worried — reassurance does not replace being seen if things change.

blocks.heading: What to document
bullets: Onset, site, and character of pain, and how it has changed.
Associated symptoms screened for (bleeding, fever, urinary symptoms, headache/visual symptoms, contractions, movements).
Examination and investigation findings; fetal assessment result.
Advice, referral route, and safety-netting given.
